claim: Hypochlorous acid (HOCl) is a powerful antimicrobial oxidant produced by neutrophils to fight infections.
source: Hypochlorous acid (HOCl), a powerful antimicrobial oxidant, is produced by neutrophils to fight infections.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by established scientific knowledge about neutrophil function.

claim: N-chlorination induced by HOCl concentrations encountered at sites of inflammation converts blood plasma proteins into chaperone-like holdases that protect other proteins from aggregation.
source: Here, we show that N-chlorination, induced by HOCl concentrations encountered at sites of inflammation, converts blood plasma proteins into chaperone-like holdases that protect other proteins from aggregation.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from aggregation assays shown in Figures 1-5.

claim: The chaperone-like conversion of plasma proteins by HOCl was reversible by antioxidants.
source: This chaperone-like conversion was reversible by antioxidants and was abrogated by prior methylation of basic amino acids.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that ascorbate treatment reversed the chaperone activity (Figures 1, 2, 5).

claim: The chaperone-like conversion of plasma proteins by HOCl was abrogated by prior methylation of basic amino acids.
source: This chaperone-like conversion was reversible by antioxidants and was abrogated by prior methylation of basic amino acids.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that methylation prevented chaperone activation (Figures 2, 5).

claim: Reversible N-chlorination of basic amino acid side chains is the major factor that converts plasma proteins into efficient activators of immune cells.
source: Furthermore, reversible N-chlorination of basic amino acid side chains is the major factor that converts plasma proteins into efficient activators of immune cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from NADPH oxidase activation assays (Figures 4, 6, 7).

claim: HOCl-modified serum albumin acts as a pro-survival molecule that protects neutrophils from cell death induced by highly immunogenic foreign antigens.
source: Finally, HOCl-modified serum albumin was found to act as a pro-survival molecule that protects neutrophils from cell death induced by highly immunogenic foreign antigens.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing reduced apoptosis in the presence of HOCl-modified HSA (Figure 8).

claim: HOCl is produced from hydrogen peroxide and chloride ions by the heme enzyme myeloperoxidase (MPO).
source: HOCl, a major inflammatory ROS, is produced from hydrogen peroxide and chloride ions by the heme enzyme myeloperoxidase (MPO) (Furtmüller et al., 1998; van Dalen et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The antimicrobial properties of HOCl are well documented.
source: The antimicrobial properties of HOCl are well documented and numerous reports have provided strong evidence for severe damage to bacterial components within the neutrophil phagosome (Chapman et al., 2002; Rosen et al., 2002; Degrossoli et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: HOCl exposure of proteins typically leads to side chain modification.
source: In proteins, HOCl exposure typically leads to side chain modification (Clark et al., 1986; Beck-Speier et al., 1988; Heinecke, 1999; Domigan et al., 1995; Sivey et al., 2013), fragmentation (Vissers and Winterbourn, 1991; Hawkins and Davies, 1998), misfolding/aggregation (Hazell et al., 1994) or intermolecular di-tyrosine cross-linking, a hallmark of HOCl-oxidized proteins (Heinecke et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: HOCl exposure of proteins can lead to fragmentation.
source: In proteins, HOCl exposure typically leads to side chain modification (Clark et al., 1986; Beck-Speier et al., 1988; Heinecke, 1999; Domigan et al., 1995; Sivey et al., 2013), fragmentation (Vissers and Winterbourn, 1991; Hawkins and Davies, 1998), misfolding/aggregation (Hazell et al., 1994) or intermolecular di-tyrosine cross-linking, a hallmark of HOCl-oxidized proteins (Heinecke et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: HOCl exposure of proteins can lead to misfolding/aggregation.
source: In proteins, HOCl exposure typically leads to side chain modification (Clark et al., 1986; Beck-Speier et al., 1988; Heinecke, 1999; Domigan et al., 1995; Sivey et al., 2013), fragmentation (Vissers and Winterbourn, 1991; Hawkins and Davies, 1998), misfolding/aggregation (Hazell et al., 1994) or intermolecular di-tyrosine cross-linking, a hallmark of HOCl-oxidized proteins (Heinecke et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Intermolecular di-tyrosine cross-linking is a hallmark of HOCl-oxidized proteins.
source: In proteins, HOCl exposure typically leads to side chain modification (Clark et al., 1986; Beck-Speier et al., 1988; Heinecke, 1999; Domigan et al., 1995; Sivey et al., 2013), fragmentation (Vissers and Winterbourn, 1991; Hawkins and Davies, 1998), misfolding/aggregation (Hazell et al., 1994) or intermolecular di-tyrosine cross-linking, a hallmark of HOCl-oxidized proteins (Heinecke et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Hsp33 is reversibly activated by HOCl through oxidation of four critical cysteine residues.
source: One of the first protective proteins to be noticed was Hsp33, which gets reversibly activated by HOCl through oxidation of four critical cysteine residues (Winter et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Cysteine thiols together with methionine residues react rapidly with HOCl.
source: This is not surprising, as cysteine thiols together with methionine residues react rapidly with HOCl (Storkey et al., 2014; Arnhold et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: E. coli RidA undergoes HOCl-based conversion into a chaperone holdase through N-chlorination of basic amino acids.
source: More recently, we found that E. coli RidA, a member of the highly conserved, but functionally diverse YjgF/YER057c/UK114 protein family, also undergoes HOCl-based conversion into a chaperone holdase. This chaperone was highly active as protector of proteins from HOCl-induced aggregation. However, in this case, instead of cysteine oxidation, N-chlorination of basic amino acids was the mechanism of its activation (Müller et al., 2014), although reactivity of HOCl with side chains of lysine and arginine is four to seven orders of magnitude lower than that of cysteine (Pattison and Davies, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research by the authors.

claim: Reactivity of HOCl with side chains of lysine and arginine is four to seven orders of magnitude lower than that of cysteine.
source: More recently, we found that E. coli RidA, a member of the highly conserved, but functionally diverse YjgF/YER057c/UK114 protein family, also undergoes HOCl-based conversion into a chaperone holdase. This chaperone was highly active as protector of proteins from HOCl-induced aggregation. However, in this case, instead of cysteine oxidation, N-chlorination of basic amino acids was the mechanism of its activation (Müller et al., 2014), although reactivity of HOCl with side chains of lysine and arginine is four to seven orders of magnitude lower than that of cysteine (Pattison and Davies, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: N-chlorination is a reversible oxidative modification that can be removed by cellular antioxidants such as ascorbate, glutathione or thioredoxin.
source: But much like cysteine oxidation, N-chlorination is a reversible oxidative modification that can be removed by cellular antioxidants such as ascorbate, glutathione or thioredoxin and thus can switch the holdase function of RidA off (Müller et al., 2014; Chesney et al., 1996; Peskin and Winterbourn, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: E. coli CnoX (YbbN), when activated via N-chlorination, binds to and prevents a variety of substrates from aggregation and being irreversible oxidized.
source: Similar observations were made more recently with E. coli CnoX (YbbN) that, when activated via N-chlorination, binds to and prevents a variety of substrates from aggregation and being irreversible oxidized (Goemans et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: During inflammatory processes, up to 30% of total cellular MPO is secreted by neutrophils into extracellular surroundings via degranulation, leakage during phagocytosis, or by association with NETs.
source: During inflammatory processes, up to 30% of total cellular MPO is secreted by neutrophils into extracellular surroundings via degranulation, leakage during phagocytosis, or by association with NETs (Parker et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Neutrophils accumulated in the interstitial fluid of inflamed tissues generate HOCl at concentrations of up to 25–50 mM/hr.
source: Neutrophils, accumulated in the interstitial fluid of inflamed tissues, have been reported to generate HOCl at concentrations of up to 25–50 mM/hr (Summers et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: HOCl can drastically increase the activity of the extracellular chaperone α2-macroglobulin (α2M) in human blood plasma to counteract the aggregation of host proteins under hypochlorous acid stress.
source: It is thus not surprising that HOCl can also drastically increase the activity of the extracellular chaperone α2-macroglobulin (α2M) in human blood plasma to counteract the aggregation of host proteins under hypochlorous acid stress (Wyatt et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The underlying molecular mechanism of HOCl-mediated conversion of α2-macroglobulin is still unclear.
source: However, the underlying molecular mechanism of HOCl-mediated conversion of this plasma protein is still unclear.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: HOCl reacts instantly with diverse biological molecules including proteins, DNA, cholesterol and lipids.
source: And while neutrophils produce high amounts of HOCl, it does not accumulate at those levels, as it reacts instantly with diverse biological molecules including proteins (Hawkins et al., 2003), DNA (Prütz, 1996), cholesterol (Carr et al., 1996) and lipids (Winterbourn et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Human serum albumin (HSA) and other plasma proteins are considered the major targets of HOCl-mediated damage and constitute the main sink for HOCl in the vicinity of inflammation.
source: But due to their high abundance in blood and interstitial fluid, human serum albumin (HSA) and other plasma proteins are considered the major targets of HOCl-mediated damage and as such constitute the main sink for HOCl in the vicinity of inflammation (Shao et al., 2006; Peng et al., 2005; Colombo et al., 2017; Himmelfarb and McMonagle, 2001; Fogh-Andersen et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Advanced oxidation protein products (AOPPs) have been employed as in vivo markers of chronic inflammation.
source: The resulting products of the reaction of plasma proteins with hypochlorous acid, known as advanced oxidation protein products (AOPPs), have, therefore, been employed as in vivo markers of chronic inflammation (Witko-Sarsat et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Accumulation of AOPPs has been first discovered in patients with chronic kidney disease.
source: Accumulation of AOPPs has been first discovered in patients with chronic kidney disease (Witko-Sarsat et al., 1996) and later also found in a variety of other inflammatory diseases, for example cardiovascular disease, neurodegenerative disorders, rheumatoid arthritis and some cancers (recently reviewed in Aratani, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: AOPPs have been found in cardiovascular disease, neurodegenerative disorders, rheumatoid arthritis and some cancers.
source: Accumulation of AOPPs has been first discovered in patients with chronic kidney disease (Witko-Sarsat et al., 1996) and later also found in a variety of other inflammatory diseases, for example cardiovascular disease, neurodegenerative disorders, rheumatoid arthritis and some cancers (recently reviewed in Aratani, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Accumulating experimental evidence supports a critical contribution of AOPPs to the progression of inflammation.
source: Accumulating experimental evidence supports a critical contribution of AOPPs to the progression of inflammation (Liu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: HOCl-modified HSA accumulates in inflammatory diseases and acts as proinflammatory mediator by increasing oxidative stress and inflammation through stimulation of leukocytes.
source: HOCl-modified HSA accumulates in inflammatory diseases and was found to act as proinflammatory mediator by increasing oxidative stress and inflammation through stimulation of leukocytes (Witko-Sarsat et al., 2003; Gorudko, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Human serum treated with a 10-fold molar excess of HOCl significantly decreases aggregation of chemically denatured citrate synthase.
source: Human serum, when treated with a 10-fold molar excess of HOCl (Human serum 10xHOCl), significantly decreases aggregation of chemically denatured citrate synthase as measured by light scattering at 360 nm.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1 with quantitative data.

claim: Reduction of HOCl-treated human serum with ascorbate reverses the chaperone-like conversion of the serum.
source: Reduction of HOCl-treated human serum with a 50-fold molar excess of the antioxidant ascorbate (Human serum 10xHOCl/Asc) reverses this chaperone-like conversion of the serum.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1 with quantitative data.

claim: The major protein component of human serum is human serum albumin (HSA).
source: The major protein component of human serum is human serum albumin (HSA).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about serum composition.

claim: Bovine serum albumin (BSA) exhibits increased chaperone activity upon treatment with HOCl.
source: Previously, we showed that its bovine homologue bovine serum albumin (BSA) exhibits increased chaperone activity upon treatment with HOCl (Müller et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research by the authors.

claim: An HOCl concentration of at least 10 mM is required for the generation of significant quantities of AOPPs in plasma.
source: An HOCl concentration of at least 10 mM has been shown to be required for the generation of significant quantities of the so-called advanced oxidation protein products (AOPPs) in plasma, associated with a number of inflammatory diseases (Witko-Sarsat et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The localized concentration of HOCl generated by accumulated neutrophils in the interstitium of chronically inflamed tissues can reach values of 25–50 mM/hr.
source: The localized concentration of HOCl generated by accumulated neutrophils in the interstitium of chronically inflamed tissues, however, can be much higher and reach values of 25–50 mM/hr (Summers et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The typical interstitial concentration of HSA is around 0.3 mM.
source: The typical interstitial concentration of HSA is assumed to be around 0.3 mM (Smith and Staples, 1982), bringing a 50-fold molar excess to 15 mM, a concentration that could reasonably be expected to be reached at confined sites of inflammation based on the propensity of neutrophils to generate HOCl (Foote et al., 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: HSA treated with 10- or 50-fold molar excess of HOCl significantly reduced the aggregation of citrate synthase.
source: HSA treated in these ways significantly reduced the aggregation of citrate synthase, showing that HSA acts as a potent chaperone in serum upon modification by HOCl (Figure 2a-d).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 2 with quantitative data.

claim: The chaperone activity of HSA was much higher upon exposure to a 50-fold molar excess of HOCl when compared to a 10-fold molar excess.
source: The chaperone activity of HSA was much higher upon exposure to a 50-fold molar excess of HOCl when compared to a 10-fold molar excess, suggesting a dose-dependent activation of the HSA chaperone function by HOCl.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 with quantitative data comparing different HOCl concentrations.

claim: H2O2 did not convert HSA into a chaperone-like holdase.
source: H2O2, another major oxidant generated by neutrophils, and a substrate for myeloperoxidase, did not convert HSA into a chaperone-like holdase (Figure 2e,f).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 2e,f with quantitative data.

claim: HOCl-treated HSA prevented the aggregation of IlvA.
source: The chaperone activity of HSA was not dependent on the substrate protein: HOCl-treated HSA also prevented the aggregation of IlvA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 with quantitative data.

claim: Full activation of the chaperone function of HSA requires a higher oxidation/chlorination level of the protein compared to bacterial RidA and Hsp33.
source: In contrast to bacterial RidA and Hsp33 (Müller et al., 2014; Winter et al., 2008), full activation of the chaperone function of HSA seems to require a higher oxidation/chlorination level of the protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the dose-dependent activation shown in Figure 2 and comparison with cited previous research.

claim: Reduction of HOCl-treated HSA with ascorbate switches off its chaperone activity.
source: Reduction of HOCl-treated HSA with a 50-fold molar excess of the antioxidant ascorbate (HSA 10xHOCl/Asc and HSA 50xHOCl/Asc) switches off its chaperone activity.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 2g,h with quantitative data.

claim: Methylation of basic amino acid side chains prior to HOCl treatment abrogates the chaperone-like conversion of HSA.
source: Methylation of basic amino acid side chains prior to HOCl treatment (HSA Met/10xHOCl and HSA Met/50xHOCl) abrogates the chaperone-like conversion of HSA.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 2i,j with quantitative data.

claim: Treatment of HSA with HOCl resulted in a dose-dependent loss of free amino groups.
source: Evidently, exposure to HOCl resulted in some loss of free amino groups. Amino group content of HSA decreased by approximately 10% after treatment with a 10-fold molar excess of HOCl (HSA 10xHOCl) and by 40% upon exposure to a 50-fold molar excess of HOCl (HSA 50xHOCl) (Figure 3a,b).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 3a,b with quantitative data from fluorescamine assays.

claim: Reduction of chlorinated HSA with ascorbate resulted in a full recovery of accessible amino groups.
source: Reduction of both chlorinated HSA samples with ascorbate resulted in a full recovery of accessible amino groups with concomitant loss of chaperone activity (Figure 2g,h).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3a,b with quantitative data.

claim: Content of N-chloramines in HSA increases with excess of HOCl.
source: A direct determination of N-chloramines showed that content of N-chloramines increases with excess of HOCl in accordance with the decrease of free amino groups.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 3c,d with quantitative data.

claim: The increase in N-chloramines in HSA was reversible by ascorbate, DTT and methionine.
source: This increase was reversible by ascorbate, DTT and methionine and virtually no chloramines were detected in samples treated with these reductants (Figure 3c,d, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3c,d and Figure 3—figure supplement 1 with quantitative data.

claim: HOCl treatment of HSA leads to an increased hydrophobicity of the protein.
source: Absolute fluorescence of 1.6 μM Nile red was higher for HSA 50xHOCl when compared with untreated HSA with a maximum at 616.5 nm (621.5 nm for native HSA) showing a blue shift in emission maximum consistent with a decreased polarity of the protein solution (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3e,f with quantitative data from Nile red fluorescence assays.

claim: The concentration at which HSA is half-saturated with Nile red dye was significantly higher for untreated HSA compared to HSA 50xHOCl.
source: The concentration of native HSA and HSA 50xHOCl, at which the proteins have been half-saturated with dye were calculated (Figure 3f). This concentration was significantly higher for untreated HSA compared to HSA 50xHOCl, pointing toward an increased hydrophobicity of HSA 50xHOCl.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3f with quantitative data.

claim: Modified HSA induces neutrophil NADPH oxidase activation reflected by an increased generation of reactive oxygen species upon exposure to high doses of HOCl.
source: Upon exposure to high doses of HOCl, as those present in chronically inflamed tissues, modified HSA was found to induce neutrophil NADPH oxidase activation reflected by an increased generation of reactive oxygen species and accompanied by degranulation (Gorudko, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Pathophysiological concentrations of HOCl can induce different modifications on plasma proteins including carbonylation, N-chlorination, cysteine and methionine oxidation or inter- and intramolecular di-tyrosine cross-linking.
source: Pathophysiological concentrations of HOCl are able to induce different modifications on plasma proteins including carbonylation, N-chlorination, cysteine and methionine oxidation or inter- and intramolecular di-tyrosine cross-linking (Clark et al., 1986; Beck-Speier et al., 1988; Domigan et al., 1995; Heinecke et al., 1993), with most of them being considered irreversible.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Most HOCl-induced modifications on plasma proteins are considered irreversible.
source: Pathophysiological concentrations of HOCl are able to induce different modifications on plasma proteins including carbonylation, N-chlorination, cysteine and methionine oxidation or inter- and intramolecular di-tyrosine cross-linking (Clark et al., 1986; Beck-Speier et al., 1988; Domigan et al., 1995; Heinecke et al., 1993), with most of them being considered irreversible.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge and citations.

claim: Differentiated PLB-985 cells acquire a neutrophil-like phenotype upon differentiation with DMSO and IFNγ.
source: For this purpose, we chose the human myeloid cell line PLB-985 that acquires a neutrophil-like phenotype upon differentiation with DMSO and IFNγ (Pivot-Pajot et al., 2010; Tlili et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Lucigenin reacts with superoxide anion radicals and hydrogen peroxide to form a light-emitting species.
source: Generation of oxidants by the NADPH oxidase was assessed by lucigenin, a well characterized and frequently used chemiluminescence probe, which reacts with superoxide anion radicals and hydrogen peroxide to form a light-emitting species (Aasen et al., 1987; Maskiewicz et al., 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Differentiated PLB-985 cells showed a low basal level of superoxide generation when incubated in buffer in the absence of any activating agents.
source: Differentiated PLB-985 cells, when incubated in buffer in the absence of any activating agents, showed a low basal level of superoxide generation resulting from IFNγ-mediated enhancement of the NADPH oxidase activity during the differentiation period (Ellison et al., 2015) (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4a and supported by a citation.

claim: Treatment of differentiated PLB-985 cells with PMA led to a drastic increase in superoxide production.
source: In line with expectations, treatment of the cells with phorbol-12-myristate-13-acetate (PMA), a known activator of neutrophil NADPH oxidase, led to a drastic increase in superoxide production and was thus used as positive control (Wolfson et al., 1985) (Figure 4a,c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4a,c and supported by a citation.

claim: Addition of untreated HSA significantly increased the generation of superoxide by >20% compared to the mock control.
source: Addition of untreated HSA significantly increased the generation of superoxide by >20% compared to the mock control.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 with quantitative data.

claim: HSA treated with a 10-fold molar excess of HOCl did not further enhance NADPH oxidase activity compared to untreated HSA.
source: No further enhancement of the NADPH oxidase activity was observed with HSA after exposure to a 10-fold molar excess of HOCl, indicating that the chosen HOCl concentration might have been too low for the conversion of HSA into a potent activator of neutrophil-like cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 with quantitative data.

claim: Cells subjected to HSA treated with a 50-fold molar excess of HOCl exhibited a substantial increase in superoxide production within the first ~25 min of incubation.
source: In contrast, cells subjected to HSA that has been treated with a 50-fold molar excess of HOCl exhibited a substantial increase in superoxide production within the first ~25 min of incubation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4a with quantitative data.

claim: NADPH oxidase activation by HSA 50xHOCl proceeded at a lower rate and was less sustained compared to PMA, returning to basal level 40 min after addition.
source: In comparison to PMA, NADPH oxidase activation by HSA 50xHOCl proceeded at a lower rate and was less sustained, returning to basal level 40 min after the addition of HSA 50xHOCl to the cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4a with quantitative data.

claim: N-chlorinated HSA can directly react with the fluorescent dye H2DCF-DA, eliciting a positive signal in the absence of cells.
source: During our experiments, we observed that N-chlorinated HSA can directly react with the fluorescent dye, 2', 7'-dichlorodihydrofluorescein diacetate (H2DCF-DA), which is the most widely used probe for measuring intracellular ROS production (Chen et al., 2010), eliciting a positive signal in the absence of cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 with quantitative data.

claim: When reduced by ascorbate, HSA 50xHOCl lost its stimulatory effect on neutrophil-like cells.
source: Importantly, when reduced by ascorbate, HSA 50xHOCl lost its stimulatory effect, showing that the functional conversion of HSA to an efficient activator of neutrophil-like cells upon HOCl exposure reflects a reversible process.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 with quantitative data.

claim: Methylation of the basic amino acids of HSA prior to HOCl treatment completely prevented HOCl-treated HSA from activating the neutrophil oxidative burst.
source: The latter finding was further corroborated by methylation of the basic amino acids of HSA prior to HOCl treatment, which completely prevented HOCl-treated HSA from activating the neutrophil oxidative burst.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 with quantitative data.

claim: Native α2-macroglobulin (α2M) acts as an extracellular chaperone that binds to and prevents the accumulation of misfolded proteins, particularly during the innate immune response.
source: Aside from its known interaction with proteases, native α2-macroglobulin (α2M) acts as an extracellular chaperone that binds to and prevents the accumulation of misfolded proteins, particularly during the innate immune response.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge about α2M function.

claim: Exposure to HOCl improves the chaperone function of α2M.
source: Exposure to HOCl was found to further improve the chaperone function of α2M, but the mechanism remained unclear (Wyatt et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Chaperone activity of α2M increased with the amount of HOCl added.
source: In line with expectations, chaperone activity of α2M increased with the amount of HOCl added (Figure 5a,b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5a,b with quantitative data.

claim: Treatment of α2M with ascorbate fully inhibited the chaperone activation of HOCl-modified α2M.
source: Treatment with ascorbate, as well as methylation of basic amino acid residues prior to HOCl exposure fully inhibited the chaperone activation of HOCl-modified α2M.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5a,b with quantitative data.

claim: Methylation of basic amino acid residues prior to HOCl exposure fully inhibited the chaperone activation of HOCl-modified α2M.
source: Treatment with ascorbate, as well as methylation of basic amino acid residues prior to HOCl exposure fully inhibited the chaperone activation of HOCl-modified α2M.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5a,b with quantitative data.

claim: Cohn fraction IV and the γ-globulin fraction exhibit chaperone-like conversion upon HOCl treatment.
source: Intriguingly, we also observed similar chaperone-like conversion upon HOCl treatment for Cohn fraction IV and the γ-globulin fraction (Figure 5c–f).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5c-f with quantitative data.

claim: Efficient activation of the chaperone activity of Cohn fraction IV and γ-globulin fraction required higher HOCl concentrations compared to HSA.
source: In both cases, however, efficient activation of the chaperone activity required higher HOCl concentrations.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5c-f with quantitative data.

claim: Exposure of Cohn fraction IV to a 50-fold molar excess of HOCl strongly activated chaperone-like properties.
source: While exposure of Cohn fraction IV to an estimated 10-fold molar excess of HOCl (corresponding to 2 mM HOCl) had only little effect on citrate synthase aggregation, treatment with a 50-fold molar excess of HOCl strongly activated chaperone-like properties (Figure 5c,d).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5c,d with quantitative data.

claim: The chaperone activity of Cohn fraction IV was markedly reduced, but not completely inhibited, after reduction with ascorbate.
source: This chaperone activity was markedly reduced, but not completely inhibited, after reduction with ascorbate.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5c,d with quantitative data.

claim: Methylation of amine side chains prior to HOCl exposure did not fully abrogate the chaperone-like conversion of Cohn fraction IV.
source: Likewise, methylation of amine side chains prior to HOCl exposure did not fully abrogate the chaperone-like conversion of this protein fraction.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5c,d with quantitative data.

claim: Activation of the chaperone function of the γ-globulin fraction occurred at HOCl concentrations ranging from 4.3 mM to 13 mM.
source: Similarly, activation of the chaperone function of the γ-globulin fraction occurred at higher HOCl concentrations ranging from 4.3 mM to 13 mM (corresponding to an estimated 50- to 150-fold molar excess of HOCl).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5e,f with quantitative data.

claim: While chaperone activity of γ-globulin fraction increased with the amount of HOCl added, reversibility of the chaperone function by ascorbate decreased.
source: Strikingly, while chaperone activity increased with the amount of HOCl added, reversibility of the chaperone function by ascorbate decreased (Figure 5e,f).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5e,f with quantitative data.

claim: At least some proteins in Cohn fraction IV and γ-globulin fraction are transformed to chaperones upon modification by HOCl.
source: These results suggest that at least some proteins in both plasma fractions tested are transformed to chaperones upon modification by HOCl.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Efficient activation of chaperone function in Cohn fraction IV and γ-globulin fraction is strongly, but not exclusively linked to N-chlorination.
source: Efficient activation of their chaperone function is strongly, but, unlike HSA, not exclusively linked to N-chlorination, suggesting some other HOCl-induced modifications that cannot be removed by ascorbate in these plasma proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the partial reversibility by ascorbate shown in Figure 5.

claim: α2-macroglobulin treated with a 50-fold molar excess of HOCl did not enhance superoxide production by differentiated PLB-985 cells.
source: Addition of α2-macroglobulin, treated with a 50-fold molar excess of HOCl (i.e. 1.5 mM HOCl), did not enhance superoxide production (Figure 6a,b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6a,b with quantitative data.

claim: Cohn fraction IV treated with a 50-fold molar excess of HOCl converted at least some proteins into highly efficient stimulators of the neutrophil NADPH oxidase.
source: In contrast, exposure to the same molar excess of HOCl, corresponding to 10 mM HOCl in this case, converted at least some proteins of Cohn fraction IV into highly efficient stimulators of the neutrophil NADPH oxidase (Figure 6c,d).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6c,d with quantitative data.

claim: Activation by HOCl-treated Cohn fraction IV occurred at a similar rate as the activation by PMA.
source: Analysis of the kinetics showed that activation by this HOCl-treated protein fraction occurred at a similar rate as the activation by PMA.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6c with quantitative data.

claim: The γ-globulin fraction treated with a 150-fold molar excess of HOCl showed a stimulatory effect on neutrophil NADPH oxidase.
source: Such a stimulatory effect was also observed for the γ-globulin fraction upon treatment with an estimated 150-fold molar excess of HOCl (i.e. 13 mM).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6e,f with quantitative data.

claim: The minimum HOCl concentration required for the activating function of Cohn fraction IV and γ-globulin fraction was 10 mM.
source: The minimum HOCl concentration required for the activating function of these plasma proteins was thus 10 mM and conformed to the range of HOCl concentrations expected under inflammatory conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The activating effect of HOCl-treated Cohn fraction IV and γ-globulin fraction was completely abolished upon reduction with ascorbate.
source: Importantly, the activating effect of both HOCl-treated plasma fractions was completely abolished upon reduction with ascorbate or by prior methylation of their amino groups, strongly suggesting that N-chlorination is the responsible mechanism for the functional switch of these proteins into efficient activators of neutrophil-like cells as well.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6 with quantitative data.

claim: The activating effect of HOCl-treated Cohn fraction IV and γ-globulin fraction was completely abolished by prior methylation of their amino groups.
source: Importantly, the activating effect of both HOCl-treated plasma fractions was completely abolished upon reduction with ascorbate or by prior methylation of their amino groups, strongly suggesting that N-chlorination is the responsible mechanism for the functional switch of these proteins into efficient activators of neutrophil-like cells as well.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6 with quantitative data.

claim: PI3K is a key component of the well-documented, anti-apoptotic PI3K/Akt signaling pathway.
source: Since PI3K is a key component of the well-documented, anti-apoptotic PI3K/Akt signaling pathway (Martelli et al., 2007), it was tempting to speculate that HOCl-modified HSA could promote cell survival in the presence of noxious stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Wortmannin strongly attenuated the HSA 50xHOCl- and IgG 150xHOCl-induced ROS generation by immune cells.
source: In contrast, wortmannin strongly attenuated the HSA 50xHOCl- and IgG 150xHOCl-induced ROS generation by the immune cells, suggesting a PI3K-dependent mechanism of NADPH oxidase activation (Figure 7a,b,d).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 with quantitative data.

claim: Pretreatment with Gö 6983 strongly inhibited NADPH oxidase activation by PMA, but not by HSA 50xHOCl and IgG 150xHOCl.
source: Along this line, pretreatment with 200 nM Gö 6983, that selectively inhibits several PKC isozyme families, including the classical PKCα and PKCβII, the novel PKCδ and the atypical PKCζ, strongly inhibited NADPH oxidase activation by PMA, but not by HSA 50xHOCl and IgG 150xHOCl.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 with quantitative data.

claim: PI3K is the key signaling component in the pathway that leads to HSA 50xHOCl- and IgG 150xHOCl-dependent activation of the neutrophil NADPH oxidase.
source: These results suggest that PI3K is the key signaling component in the pathway that leads to HSA 50xHOCl- and IgG 150xHOCl-dependent activation of the neutrophil NADPH oxidase.
evidence: This is inferred from the inhibitor experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: The mycolyltransferase Ag85B is the major antigen produced and secreted from all mycobacterial species during infection.
source: The mycolyltransferase Ag85B is the major antigen produced and secreted from all mycobacterial species during infection (Belisle et al., 1997) and has been shown to play an important role in the induction of protective immunity (Andersen, 1994; Baldwin et al., 1998) by inducing strong T cell proliferation and IFN-γ secretion (Launois et al., 1994; Takamura et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Ag85B plays an important role in the induction of protective immunity by inducing strong T cell proliferation and IFN-γ secretion.
source: The mycolyltransferase Ag85B is the major antigen produced and secreted from all mycobacterial species during infection (Belisle et al., 1997) and has been shown to play an important role in the induction of protective immunity (Andersen, 1994; Baldwin et al., 1998) by inducing strong T cell proliferation and IFN-γ secretion (Launois et al., 1994; Takamura et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Activation of neutrophils during mycobacterial infections is often accompanied by accelerated apoptosis.
source: Activation of neutrophils during mycobacterial infections is often accompanied by accelerated apoptosis (Alemán et al., 2002; Perskvist et al., 2002), but the mechanism by which mycobacterial species or their secreted antigens induce apoptosis has not been elucidated in detail.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Staurosporine has been characterized as an efficient inducer of apoptosis in various cell types via caspase-dependent and -independent pathways.
source: Staurosporine, a protein kinase inhibitor, has been characterized as an efficient inducer of apoptosis in various cell types via caspase-dependent and -independent pathways (Chae et al., 2000; Zhang et al., 2004) and thus, was also used as an cell death-promoting agent in our experiments.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Upon treatment with Ag85B, the ratio of viable cells to early/late apoptotic cells has markedly decreased compared to the control cells.
source: Upon treatment with Ag85B, the ratio of viable cells to early/late apoptotic cells has markedly decreased compared to the control cells, that were incubated in the absence of Ag85B, pointing toward a lifetime-limiting effect of Ag85B.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8 with flow cytometry data.

claim: Pretreatment with Z-VAD-FMK did not significantly affect Ag85B-induced cell death.
source: Pretreatment with the broad-spectrum pan-caspase inhibitor Z-VAD-FMK did not significantly affect Ag85B-induced cell death, suggesting that Ag85B exerts its lethal effect through a caspase-independent mechanism.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8 with flow cytometry data.

claim: Reduction of the cells' phagocytic capacity by cytochalasin D resulted in markedly improved cell survival in the presence of Ag85B.
source: To test whether the toxicity of Ag85B depends on its uptake by the immune cells, we pretreated the cells with cytochalasin D, an inhibitor of phagocytosis, prior to the addition of Ag85B. Reduction of the cells' phagocytic capacity resulted in markedly improved cell survival in the presence of Ag85B.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8 with flow cytometry data.

claim: Pretreatment with HOCl-modified HSA completely prevented cell death upon addition of Ag85B.
source: Remarkably, pretreatment with HOCl-modified HSA, added at a 155-fold molar excess over Ag85B, completely prevented cell death upon addition of Ag85B.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8 with flow cytometry data.

claim: Native HSA had almost no effect on Ag85B-induced cell death.
source: In contrast, native HSA had almost no effect on Ag85B-induced cell death.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8 with flow cytometry data.

claim: Z-VAD-FMK, but not HOCl-treated HSA was able to significantly reduce staurosporine-induced apoptosis.
source: In support of this conclusion, Z-VAD-FMK, but not HOCl-treated HSA was able to significantly reduce staurosporine-induced apoptosis.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8 with flow cytometry data.

claim: When combined with staurosporine, HOCl-modified HSA triggered necrosis with the majority of the cells being Annexin V and PI positive.
source: Instead, when combined with staurosporine, HOCl-modified HSA triggered necrosis with the majority of the cells being Annexin V and PI positive.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8 with flow cytometry data.

claim: HOCl-modified HSA significantly reduced the aggregation of Ag85B when added at an 80-fold molar excess over the protein.
source: When denatured Ag85B was diluted into buffer, it readily formed aggregates (Figure 9a,b). This aggregation could not be prevented by untreated HSA. Presence of HOCl-modified HSA, however, significantly reduced the aggregation of Ag85B when added at a 80-fold molar excess over the protein.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9a,b with quantitative data.

claim: Reduction of HOCl-modified HSA with ascorbate fully abrogated its ability to bind Ag85B.
source: Again, reduction with ascorbate fully abrogated HSA HOCl's ability to bind Ag85B.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9a,b with quantitative data.

claim: Cells co-incubated with native HSA accumulated around 30% less Ag85B compared to cells treated with Ag85B alone.
source: Cells co-incubated with native HSA accumulated around 30% less Ag85B compared to cells treated with Ag85B alone (Figure 9c,d).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9c,d with flow cytometry data.

claim: Presence of HOCl-treated HSA reduced uptake of Ag85B by up to 80%.
source: But presence of HOCl-treated HSA reduced uptake of Ag85B by up to 80%.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9c,d with flow cytometry data.

claim: Sustained cell viability in the presence of Ag85B is most likely linked to decreased antigen uptake by the immune cells.
source: Sustained cell viability in the presence of Ag85B is thus most likely linked to decreased antigen uptake by the immune cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figures 8 and 9.

claim: HOCl-mediated conversion of plasma proteins into potent chaperones depends primarily on reversible chlorination of their basic amino acids.
source: Here, we provide direct evidence that HOCl-mediated conversion of plasma proteins into potent chaperones depends primarily on reversible chlorination of their basic amino acids.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple experimental results.

claim: Treatment of HSA with HOCl led to dose-dependent reduction of the accessible amino group content accompanied by an increase in N-chloramine content and surface hydrophobicity.
source: Along this line, treatment of HSA with HOCl led to dose-dependent reduction of the accessible amino group content accompanied by an increase in N-chloramine content and surface hydrophobicity, providing an obvious explanation for the increased affinity to unfolding proteins of N-chlorinated plasma proteins.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: N-chlorination does not irreversibly alter the structural and functional properties of a protein.
source: Since N-chlorination does not irreversibly alter the structural and functional properties of a protein, this reversible post-translational modification provides a new strategy to recruit new chaperone-like proteins on demand in response to HOCl-stress in order to minimize self-damage associated with the formation of protein aggregates during inflammation.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data showing reversibility by antioxidants.

claim: HOCl-oxidized low-density lipoproteins and HOCl-modified HSA elicit various polymorphonuclear leukocyte (PMNL) responses such as NADPH-dependent generation of ROS, degranulation or shape change.
source: For example, HOCl-oxidized low-density lipoproteins (Kopprasch et al., 1998), as well as HOCl-modified HSA (Gorudko, 2014; Witko-Sarsat et al., 1998) have been shown to elicit various polymorphonuclear leukocyte (PMNL) responses such as the NADPH-dependent generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), degranulation or shape change (Gorudko, 2014), but the mechanism for the HOCl-mediated functional conversion into a potent activator of human PMNLs remained unclear.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Reversible HOCl-mediated N-chlorination is the principal mechanism of turning plasma proteins into critical modulators of the innate immune response.
source: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study which demonstrates that reversible HOCl-mediated N-chlorination is the principal mechanism of turning plasma proteins into critical modulators of the innate immune response.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple experimental results.

claim: Gorudko (2014) reported that the phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) inhibitor wortmannin inhibited the stimulating effect of HOCl-modified HSA on immune cells.
source: Gorudko (2014) reported that the phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) inhibitor wortmannin inhibited the stimulating effect of HOCl-modified HSA on immune cells.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: PI3K and its downstream effectors, such as the serine/threonine kinase Akt, are considered to play a key role in the regulation of the neutrophil NADPH oxidase.
source: PI3K and its downstream effectors, such as the serine/threonine kinase Akt, are indeed considered to play a key role in the regulation of the neutrophil NADPH oxidase (Kennedy and DeLeo, 2008; Hawkins et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: N-chlorinated HSA can irreversibly bind to and block the major high-density lipoprotein receptor, scavenger receptor class B, type 1 (SR-BI).
source: In support of this theory, it has been reported that N-chlorinated, but not native HSA can irreversibly bind to and block the major high-density lipoprotein receptor, scavenger receptor class B, type 1 (SR-BI) (Binder et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The PI3K/Akt pathway is considered an anti-apoptotic pathway.
source: The PI3K/Akt pathway is also considered an anti-apoptotic pathway (Zhuang et al., 2011; Chang et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neutrophils are typically short-lived, but their apoptosis can be delayed both by microbial products and by various proinflammatory stimuli.
source: Neutrophils are typically short-lived, but their apoptosis can be delayed both by microbial products and by various proinflammatory stimuli (Lee et al., 1993; Colotta et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: HOCl-modified HSA can bind and neutralize proteins from HIV and West Nile virus.
source: A similar phenomenon was observed in other studies, where HOCl-modified HSA was shown to bind and neutralize proteins from HIV and West Nile virus (Vossmann et al., 2008; Speth et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Stimulation of neutrophil respiratory burst and enhanced neutrophil survival may be beneficial for pathogen elimination at the initial stage of infection.
source: Although stimulation of neutrophil respiratory burst and enhanced neutrophil survival may be beneficial for pathogen elimination at the initial stage of infection, it can eventually perpetuate a positive feedback loop and contribute to the development and progression of chronic inflammation (Figure 10).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results and illustrated in Figure 10.

claim: Stimulation of neutrophil respiratory burst and enhanced neutrophil survival can eventually perpetuate a positive feedback loop and contribute to the development and progression of chronic inflammation.
source: Although stimulation of neutrophil respiratory burst and enhanced neutrophil survival may be beneficial for pathogen elimination at the initial stage of infection, it can eventually perpetuate a positive feedback loop and contribute to the development and progression of chronic inflammation (Figure 10).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results and illustrated in Figure 10.

claim: Secretion of HOCl and other oxidants by permanently activated neutrophils leads to the destruction of neighboring, healthy cells resulting in tissue injury.
source: Secretion of HOCl and other oxidants by permanently activated neutrophils leads not only to the destruction of neighboring, healthy cells resulting in tissue injury (Pechous, 2017; Weiss, 1989; Margaroli et al., 2019), but generates more N-chlorinated plasma proteins.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Cell death and the subsequent recognition of dying neutrophils by macrophages has a critical function in the resolution of the inflammatory response.
source: Similarly, the pro-survival effect of N-chlorinated HSA is not only positive, as cell death and the subsequent recognition of dying neutrophils by macrophages has a critical function in the resolution of the inflammatory response and is strictly required to protect the surrounding tissue and prevent pathological sequelae (Erwig and Henson, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Ascorbate and glutathione in plasma can reduce N-chlorination and provide a mechanism to contain the immune reaction at the site of inflammation.
source: The presence of antioxidants such as ascorbate and glutathione in plasma, both of which can reduce N-chlorination, provide a mechanism to contain the immune reaction at the site of inflammation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing reversibility by antioxidants and established knowledge about antioxidant function.

claim: Depletion of antioxidants is often associated with chronic inflammation and other diseases.
source: Indeed, depletion of these antioxidants is often associated with chronic inflammation and other diseases (Bonham et al., 1999; Ruan et al., 1997; Huijskens et al., 2016; Rose et al., 2012) and antioxidant therapy such as high-dose intravenous vitamin C treatment leads to decrease of inflammation markers such as CRP (Mikirova et al., 2012; Carr and Cook, 2018; Block et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Antioxidant therapy such as high-dose intravenous vitamin C treatment leads to decrease of inflammation markers such as CRP.
source: Indeed, depletion of these antioxidants is often associated with chronic inflammation and other diseases (Bonham et al., 1999; Ruan et al., 1997; Huijskens et al., 2016; Rose et al., 2012) and antioxidant therapy such as high-dose intravenous vitamin C treatment leads to decrease of inflammation markers such as CRP (Mikirova et al., 2012; Carr and Cook, 2018; Block et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Reversible N-chlorination of plasma proteins turns them into effective chaperons, which can prevent the formation of protein aggregates and their uptake by immune cells, enhancing the survival of neutrophils in the presence of toxic antigens.
source: Reversible N-chlorination of these proteins turns them into effective chaperons, which can prevent the formation of protein aggregates and their uptake by immune cells, enhancing the survival of neutrophils in the presence of toxic antigens.
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 10 and supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: N-chlorinated plasma proteins activate more immune cells, which then in turn produce more HOCl, leading to the formation of more N-chlorinated plasma proteins.
source: N-chlorinated plasma proteins also activate more immune cells, which then in turn produce more HOCl, leading to the formation of more N-chlorinated plasma proteins.
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 10 and supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The positive feedback loop involving N-chlorinated plasma proteins can be attenuated and deactivated by antioxidants present in plasma, such as ascorbate and reduced glutathione (GSH).
source: This positive feedback loop can be attenuated and deactivated by antioxidants present in plasma, such as ascorbate and reduced glutathione (GSH).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 10 and supported by experimental data showing reversibility by antioxidants.

claim: HOCl-mediated N-chlorination of plasma proteins plays a critical role during inflammatory processes.
source: In summary, our data support a critical role for HOCl-mediated N-chlorination of plasma proteins during inflammatory processes and suggest that it is the critical modification mediating the physiological effects of so-called AOPPs.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple experimental results.

claim: N-chlorination is the critical modification mediating the physiological effects of AOPPs.
source: In summary, our data support a critical role for HOCl-mediated N-chlorination of plasma proteins during inflammatory processes and suggest that it is the critical modification mediating the physiological effects of so-called AOPPs.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple experimental results.

claim: The reversible conversion of HOCl-modified plasma proteins to effective chaperones confers protection against HOCl-induced protein aggregation.
source: Although the reversible conversion of HOCl-modified plasma proteins to effective chaperones confers protection against HOCl-induced protein aggregation, the increase of their immunogenicity can potentially exacerbate self-damage at sites of inflammation through a positive feedback loop.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The increase of immunogenicity of HOCl-modified plasma proteins can potentially exacerbate self-damage at sites of inflammation through a positive feedback loop.
source: Although the reversible conversion of HOCl-modified plasma proteins to effective chaperones confers protection against HOCl-induced protein aggregation, the increase of their immunogenicity can potentially exacerbate self-damage at sites of inflammation through a positive feedback loop.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The activation of immune cells by N-chlorinated plasma proteins is mediated through N-chlorination, a modification that is reversible by antioxidants present in plasma.
source: The fact that the activation of immune cells is mediated through N-chlorination, a modification that is reversible by antioxidants present in plasma, provides a mechanism to attenuate or deactivate this positive feedback loop.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.
